newsitem.title: USA: Blair, Clinton condemn Belfast explosion.
newsitem.headline: Blair, Clinton condemn Belfast explosion.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton and British Prime Minister Tony Blair on Saturday condemned a car bomb in Belfast that occurred as Group of Seven leaders met in Denver to discuss global issues, including terrorism.

"This is another appalling terrorist act and it simply underlines the need to move this (Northern Ireland peace) process forward," Blair told reporters as he met Clinton on the sidelines of the summit.

The explosion, which set a car on fire in south-central Belfast and injured three people, occurred at a tense time in Northern Ireland and followed the Irish Republican Army's killing of two policemen on Monday.

A British spokesman in Denver told reporters that it was unclear who was behind the explosion, adding that one theory was that it was set by Protestant Loyalists opposed to ending British rule in Northern Ireland.
However, both Blair and Clinton singled out Sinn Fein, the political wing of the IRA, in their remarks and called on it to stop the violence in order to be accepted at peace talks.
"I was appalled at the murders of the two officers just a few days ago. I deplore this act today, but I frankly think now the ball is in Sinn Fein's court," Clinton told reporters.
"Everybody has decisions to make in life. Their decision is, are they going to be part of this peace process or not. I hope the answer will be yes," he added.

Blair, who wants to persuade Americans to stop supporting the IRA, added: "What is essential is for Sinn Fein and everyone else to realise that if they want to be part of this process they have got to engage in purely democratic means."
The two leaders broke away from the summit sessions for a previously scheduled meeting, spending the full 20 minutes of the discussion on Northern Ireland, a U.S. official said.

Although Blair referred to the bombing as a "terrorist" act, neither leader would say whether they had any specific information on who had set the explosion in a neighbourhood near Belfast's university and city hospital.

The Northern Ireland conflict pits the IRA and others who wish to end British rule of the province against Protestant Loyalists who want to remain part of Britain. Some 3,200 people have been killed in the conflict over the past three decades.
